title: Toyota orders workers to train humanoid robots but says humans won't be replaced
gist: Toyota plans to invest $6.42 billion annually starting in 2028 to deploy 400,000 factory robots (150,000 in its own plants, 250,000 at group suppliers), using humans to train its wheeled ELEY humanoid robots via finger-mimicking 'jigs' rather than replacing the 18,000-strong veteran workforce outright.

insights.claim: Starting in 2028, Toyota Motor group plans to invest $6.42 billion every year upgrading factories with a new robotic workforce, aiming for 400,000 total robots: 150,000 in its own automotive plants and 250,000 at group company facilities producing components and materials.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A near-$6.5B/year, multi-year capex commitment signals a major industrial-automation buyer for robotics/actuator/sensor suppliers to Toyota's supply chain.
insights.quote: the Toyota Motor group aims to start investing $6.42 billion every year in upgrading factories with the new robotic workforce, according to Nikkei Asia
insights.locator: Starting in 2028, the Toyota Motor group aims to start investing

insights.claim: Toyota has already begun deploying its ELEY humanoid robots, which roll on wheels and have two hands, on assembly lines, with human workers wearing finger-shaped 'jigs' to teach the robots precise hand movements.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Imitation-learning-via-jig is a concrete, low-tech data-collection method for humanoid manipulation training that other manufacturers could replicate or that could become a market for wearable teaching-hardware vendors.
insights.quote: workers are teaching the robots, which roll around on wheels, to perform tasks requiring precise hand movements by wearing “jigs” based on the humanoids’ fingers
insights.locator: Toyota has already begun deploying some of its ELEY humanoid robots

insights.claim: A Toyota executive vice president, Hiroki Nakajima, stated the company's aim is for robots to coexist with humans rather than replace the 18,000 veteran workers across Toyota's 60 factories worldwide (including 11 US plants).
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Corporate messaging is framing automation as augmentation to manage labor-union and political backlash risk even while committing tens of billions to robot deployment; watch for divergence between stated intent and actual headcount trends.
insights.quote: a world where robots coexist with humans, rather than replacing them
insights.locator: But Hiroki Nakajima, a Toyota executive vice president

insights.claim: China deployed 2 million industrial robots in 2024, more than four times Japan's 450,500, while the US and South Korea trailed far behind at 34,200 and 30,600 respectively, according to the International Federation of Robotics.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: China's overwhelming lead in industrial robot deployment (roughly 4x Japan, ~60x the US) underscores a structural manufacturing-automation gap investors should factor into China-vs-US industrial competitiveness comparisons.
insights.quote: China alone deployed 2 million industrial robots in 2024, with Japan coming in second at 450,500 robots
insights.locator: China alone deployed 2 million industrial robots in 2024

insights.claim: The automotive industry's shift toward general-purpose humanoid robots (versus traditional fixed robotic arms) is a recent trend, driven by the bet that humanoids can flexibly handle many tasks in workplaces already designed for humans.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The thesis underpinning humanoid robot investment (Tesla Optimus, Figure, Boston Dynamics Atlas, etc.) is compatibility with human-built infrastructure rather than task-specific efficiency, a key differentiator vs. legacy industrial robotics investment.
insights.locator: The automotive industry’s turn toward humanoid robots is a more recent trend

insights.claim: Major AI and robotic hardware challenges remain, including safety around humans and uncertain cost-effectiveness versus human labor, and robotics companies have only recently begun attempting mass production of humanoid robots.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Mass production of humanoids is still nascent industry-wide, implying supply-chain and yield risk for any investor betting on near-term humanoid robot revenue ramps.
insights.locator: But many AI and robotic hardware challenges remain

themes.theme: Competitive humanoid robot race among automakers

insights.claim: Chinese EV makers Xpeng and Nio are developing or investing in their own humanoid robots, alongside Toyota and Hyundai.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A broad field of automakers (Toyota, Hyundai, Xpeng, Nio) simultaneously building humanoid robot capability signals an emerging cross-industry arms race in factory automation with multiple potential customers/investors for humanoid robotics suppliers.
insights.locator: Many automakers are developing or investing in their own humanoid robots

insights.claim: Hyundai plans to deploy Boston Dynamics-developed Atlas humanoid robots starting in 2028, targeting up to 25,000 robots across Hyundai and Kia plants worldwide within a few years, and Boston Dynamics opened a new robotics training center at Hyundai's Metaplant America facility in Georgia on September 21 to train Atlas on automotive parts sequencing tasks.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Hyundai/Boston Dynamics' concrete 2028 deployment target and dedicated Georgia training center make this one of the most trackable near-term humanoid-robot commercialization milestones in the auto sector.
insights.locator: On September 21, Boston Dynamics announced it had launched a new robotics training center
